_note: Comparative legislation references FOREIGN instruments (Kenya, Mauritius, Estonia, Korea). amategeko.gov.rw only holds Rwandan law, so these curated comparative summaries are the one dataset not scraped from it. In a production system this corpus would be fed from the East-African / Commonwealth legislative databases named in docs/04-data-and-integrations.md §35. relatedBillId points at a real draft or a real scraped law where applicable.

topics.name: Data protection & cross-border transfer
topics.description: How peer jurisdictions structure lawful bases for processing, breach notification and cross-border transfer of personal data.

countries.provisionSummary: Establishes an independent Data Commissioner; requires registration of data controllers and processors above a threshold.
countries.approachNote: Independent regulator model with a registration regime, unlike a ministry-hosted authority.

countries.provisionSummary: GDPR-aligned; transfers allowed only to countries with adequate protection or with the Commissioner's authorisation.
countries.approachNote: Adequacy + prior authorisation, stricter than standard contractual clauses alone.

countries.provisionSummary: Direct application of the EU GDPR; breach notification within 72 hours to the Data Protection Inspectorate.
countries.approachNote: Supranational harmonisation — the 72-hour standard the draft mirrors.

countries.provisionSummary: One of the strictest consent regimes; mandatory notification to affected individuals and the PIPC.
countries.approachNote: Consent-centric with dual notification (regulator and individuals).

topics.aiTakeaway: The 72-hour breach-notification window in the draft aligns with the Estonian/GDPR and Kenyan approaches; the main divergence among peers is whether the supervisory body is a fully independent commissioner (KE, MU) or hosted within government (as the draft's Digital Governance Authority currently is).

topics.name: AI accountability & automated decisions
topics.description: Emerging approaches to human oversight of automated decision-making and accountability for public-sector AI.

countries.provisionSummary: Policy-level principles (transparency, fairness) rather than binding review obligations.
countries.approachNote: Strategy-first, not yet statutory — Rwanda's draft would be ahead in creating binding duties.

countries.provisionSummary: Advisory AI Council; sectoral guidance rather than a horizontal accountability statute.
countries.approachNote: Institutional advisory model instead of enforceable per-institution officers.

countries.provisionSummary: Emphasis on a legal-person status debate and government algorithm registers.
countries.approachNote: Transparency-register approach — a complementary tool the draft omits.

countries.provisionSummary: Risk-tiered obligations; high-impact AI requires impact assessment and human oversight.
countries.approachNote: Risk-tiering — the draft's 'high-impact system' officer duty resembles this but lacks the impact-assessment step.

topics.aiTakeaway: The draft's requirement of a human-review step and an AI Accountability Officer is comparatively strong — most peers are still at strategy level. The notable gap versus Korea's Framework Act is the absence of a formal risk-tiered impact assessment before deployment.

topics.name: Electronic transactions & signatures
topics.description: Legal recognition of electronic documents and signatures across comparable jurisdictions.

countries.instrument: Kenya Information and Communications Act (E-transactions Part)
countries.provisionSummary: Recognises electronic records and advanced electronic signatures; functional-equivalence approach.
countries.approachNote: Functional equivalence, closely comparable to the Rwandan law.

countries.provisionSummary: Tiered signature reliability with accreditation of certification authorities.
countries.approachNote: Formal CA accreditation regime, more prescriptive on reliability.

countries.provisionSummary: Qualified electronic signatures with legal equivalence to handwritten ones; national eID backbone.
countries.approachNote: State eID infrastructure underpins signatures — an ecosystem the law alone doesn't create.

countries.provisionSummary: Abolished the monopoly of the national certificate; technology-neutral recognition.
countries.approachNote: Technology-neutrality after de-monopolisation — a modernisation reference point.

topics.aiTakeaway: Rwanda's functional-equivalence model matches Kenya's closely. The clearest lesson from Estonia and Korea is that signature law is only as effective as the surrounding eID/certification infrastructure and technology-neutrality — an implementation gap rather than a drafting one.
